title: How Art Pastels Revealed the True Face of Mars
description: Before computers processed the first close-up data from Mars, NASA engineers hand-colored a pixel printout using pastels. Mariner 4 revealed a cold, cratered world instead of a living planet.

beats.text: Engineers hand-colored the first photo of Mars using art pastels.
beats.visual: JPL engineers hand-colored numerical printout of Mariner 4 Mars image, 1965
queries: Mariner 4 hand colored Mars image JPL

beats.text: JPL scientists couldn't wait hours for computers to process Mariner 4's data.
beats.visual: Photograph of Mariner 4 spacecraft in cleanroom before launch, 1964

beats.text: People expected to see liquid canals and signs of alien civilization.
beats.visual: Historical map of Martian canals by Percival Lowell, 1895

beats.text: So engineers pinned numerical printouts to a wall and painted each pixel.
beats.visual: JPL team members coloring raw data strips on wall, 1965
queries: Mariner 4 hand colored Mars image JPL

beats.text: The completed drawing didn't reveal a lush, living alien world.
beats.visual: First close-up photograph frame 01 taken by Mariner 4, 1965

beats.text: Instead, it showed a dead, frozen surface covered in ancient craters.
beats.visual: Mariner 4 photograph showing cratered surface of Mars, 1965

beats.text: That simple paper image changed our vision of Mars forever.
beats.visual: Completed hand-colored pastel image of Mars by JPL staff, 1965
queries: Mariner 4 hand colored Mars image JPL
